newsitem.title: UK: British funds' enthusiasm for Japan wanes - Merrill.
newsitem.headline: British funds' enthusiasm for Japan wanes - Merrill.

text.p: British fund managers' enthusiasm for Japanese equities is on the wane and they are the closest they have been since 1992 to turning sellers of the market, according to Merrill Lynch's monthly survey of investors.
"Bulls exceeded bears by a balance of nine percent on a three month view (23 percent last month)," Merrill strategist Bijal Shah said on Monday.
On a one month view, the balance of buyers over sellers in the Japanese equity market among British fund managers who control 1.8 billion pounds in assets was just one percent, Shah said.
In the U.S. equity market, which has broken record high after record high this year, perceptions that Wall Street is set for a meltdown appear to be less prevalent.
A balance of seven percent of fund managers are looking to reduce their holdings compared with nine percent wanting to sell in October and 13 percent sellers in September.

For Britain's equity market, where the blue chip FT-SE 100 index notched a closing high of 4,073.2 points on October 21 and has since subsided after a rise in interest rates, the picture is different.
Enthusiasm for the market has peaked and a balance of four percent of the funds are looking to sell after and equal number of bulls and bears last month.
"What we are seeing is the reallocation of money from Britain to overseas assets," said Merrill's Shah.

However, most are sanguine on the outlook for the British economy, with 84 percent of managers expecting an improvement in conditions, although they expect this to be accompanied by rising inflation and interest rates.

The consensus from the fund managers surveyed is for Britain's retail price inflation to rise to an annual 3.4 percent by the end of 1997, compared with expectations of a rise to 3.2 percent by end-1997 in the October survey.
They see UK bank base rates at 6.8 percent by the end of 1997, compared with six percent now.

Funds are still heavy buyers of continental European equities, plus 15 percent are bulls after plus 16 last month, while sentiment towards the Pacific Basin has slumped to a balance of five percent being sellers, the lowest reading ever recorded by the survey.
In fixed income markets, fund managers remain buyers of British bonds, or gilts, with a balance of 11 percent planning increase exposure.

Interest in British property, which had rallied after a prolonged slump in the early 1990s has started to fall again with the balance of buyers over sellers slidind to plus one percent from plus four in October and plus 11 in September.
The Merrill survey also shows that fund managers are reducing their holdings of cash, contrary to perceptions that many large funds were selling financial assets and holding cash.
"People are still pretty sanguine over the outlook for U.S. interest rates, so there is no need to sell assets," said Merrill's Shah.
